guidance: Food scraps, egg shells, fruit peels, and leftovers are biodegradable organic matter and belong in the wet/organic green bin for composting.
tip: Keep a small counter-top compost bin with a lid to easily separate food scraps and eggshells before they mix with dry waste.

guidance: Garden clippings, dry leaves, and cut flowers are organic and compostable, and belong in the wet/organic waste stream.
tip: Mix dry brown leaves with wet green clippings to accelerate natural aerobic composting.

guidance: Used tea leaves and coffee grounds are organic matter and belong in the wet bin; they provide nitrogen-rich nutrients for compost.
tip: Check if the tea bag has a metal staple or synthetic mesh — remove it before composting the tea contents.

guidance: Paper that is heavily stained with food grease or oils cannot be recycled at paper mills and belongs in wet/compost waste.
tip: Tear off the clean lid of the pizza box for dry recycling, and put only the greasy bottom base in the wet bin.

guidance: Never pour cooking oil or melted fat down kitchen sinks. Small amounts can be absorbed into food scraps or collected for biodiesel recycling.
tip: Pour cooled oil into a sealed jar or soak it into cardboard/newspaper scraps before composting or specialized recycling.

guidance: Clean, dry paper, cardboard packaging, and newspapers are highly recyclable and belong in the dry waste bin.
tip: Flatten boxes and remove plastic packing tape to maximize recycling capacity at sorting facilities.

guidance: Glass bottles and jars are 100% endlessly recyclable dry waste. If broken, it remains recyclable but requires safe wrapping.
tip: Wrap broken glass securely in thick newspaper and write 'BROKEN GLASS' so sanitation workers avoid injury.

guidance: Rigid plastic bottles, jugs, and containers (PET #1, HDPE #2, PP #5) are recyclable dry waste.
tip: Empty and give containers a quick water rinse — food residue can spoil an entire bin batch at the recycler.

guidance: Aluminum cans, tin food cans, and clean aluminum foil are infinitely recyclable metals that save 95% energy compared to raw mining.
tip: Scrunch clean foil into a ball (at least golf-ball sized) so automated sorting machinery doesn't blow it away.

guidance: Tetra Paks contain paperboard, polyethylene, and aluminum layers that are recyclable at dedicated hydrapulping mills.
tip: Flatten the carton and push the straw or screw the cap back inside so all pieces are processed together.

guidance: Soft flexible plastic bags and LDPE film can be recycled, though many municipal curbside programs prefer collection at grocery drop-off bins.
tip: Gather multiple clean plastic bags together and stuff them inside one bag before dry disposal.

guidance: Clean textiles and wearable garments should be donated or sent to fabric shredding/upcycling channels rather than landfills.
tip: Donate gently used clothing to charities or repurpose old cotton shirts into reusable household cleaning rags.

guidance: Batteries contain corrosive acids and toxic heavy metals (lead, cadmium, lithium) that cause severe soil and groundwater contamination.
tip: Tape over battery terminals with clear tape to prevent short circuits and drop them at designated collection points.

guidance: Expired drugs and blister packs can contaminate water treatment systems and encourage antimicrobial resistance if thrown in regular trash.
tip: Return unused/expired medicines to take-back boxes at participating pharmacies and local clinics.

guidance: Chemical solvents, paints, pesticides, and pressurized aerosol cans are flammable, toxic, and hazardous.
tip: Never puncture aerosol cans. Use the entire product up or take half-full cans to local household hazardous waste centers.

guidance: Sanitary hygiene products and medical dressings contain biological materials and must be wrapped separately for sanitary incineration.
tip: Wrap sanitary waste securely in newspaper and mark with a red dot or label before putting in sanitary disposal.

guidance: CFL bulbs and fluorescent tubes contain mercury vapor, which is a neurotoxin. They must not be smashed or put in standard bins.
tip: Store intact in original packaging or bubble wrap until you can drop it at a specialized hazardous waste depot.

guidance: Extremely toxic, caustic, explosive, or carcinogenic industrial materials must never be mixed with regular municipal or recyclable trash.
tip: Store in sealed, corrosion-proof chemical containers and arrange specialized pickup with certified hazardous material handlers.

bin_name: Specialized Radioactive / Nuclear Disposal (DO NOT BIN)
guidance: Radioactive elements and nuclear substances emit ionizing radiation. They pose extreme public health risks and must NEVER be placed in any household or municipal waste bin.
tip: Contact national atomic energy or hazardous environmental regulatory authorities immediately for certified containment protocols.

guidance: Electronics and electrical accessories contain precious metals (gold, copper) alongside hazardous flame retardants and must go to certified e-waste recyclers.
tip: Look for electronics take-back bins at major retailers or municipal e-waste drive drop-offs.

guidance: Small and large broken household electrical appliances are classified as e-waste and contain recyclable copper coils and steel casing.
tip: Check if local appliance dealers offer exchange discounts when purchasing a replacement unit.
